stem: The volume of a rectangular prism is {=v} cm$^3$. The height of the prism is multiplied by a constant factor of {=k}, while its length and breadth stay the same. Calculate the volume of the new prism, in cm$^3$.
solution: The volume of a rectangular prism is given by $V=l\times b\times h$, so for the original prism $l\times b\times h={=v}$.
If the height is multiplied by a constant factor of {=k}, the new volume is $V_{\text{new}}=l\times b\times({=k}h)={=k}\times(l\times b\times h)={=k}V$.
So the volume of the prism increases by a factor of {=k}: $V_{\text{new}}={=k}\times{=v}={=k*v}$ cm$^3$.
notes: Entry point of the skill: ONE dimension scaled by a constant factor, so the volume is scaled by that same factor (book Ex 13.6 Q4 steps down to a single dimension). The original volume is given instead of the dimensions so the student must use the factor idea (V_new = k x V) rather than recompute from three lengths; the book's own questions are likewise abstract (no dimensions). The dimension scaled is always the height, so no instance is ambiguous. The original volume is any whole number of cm^3; no integer dimensions are implied or needed. Surface area is deliberately not asked here: with only one or two dimensions scaled the surface area is not a single constant multiple of the original, so a 'factor' only exists when all three dimensions are scaled (see the advanced family). Answer is the bare number of cm^3 (the stem names the unit).
